transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-09
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jose Ramirez (Redwood SE), Ellen Park (Redwood CSM), Priya Nair (Delta Labs Head of ML), Tom Barrett (Platform), Anika Sood (Security), Luca Marino (SRE)

Summary:
Delta Labs is evaluating options between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private for inference of a multimodal assistant used internally and in a B2B product. Primary concerns: strict tenant isolation, burst capacity for monthly marketing spikes (10-15x baseline during launches), predictable tail latencies for SLAs, and integration with existing KMS and SSO. The call captured requirements, current infra, and an outline for a short benchmark and follow-up deep-dive.

Topics:
- Current stack and traffic shape
- Isolation and compliance needs (VPC, per-customer tenancy)
- Reserved GPU sizing, burst pool strategy, warm-up/cold-start considerations
- Autoscale policies, graceful fallback, model variants & quantization tradeoffs
- Next steps: pricing, runbook, and technical deep-dive scheduling

Action items (spoken):
- Maya: send pricing + isolation playbook
- Jose: prepare benchmark checklist and telemetry requirements
- Priya: share traffic profile and SLOs

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, can we do quick intros? i'm maya from redwood ai i'm the ae on the account, jose is our se and ellen will help on onboarding ops.
[00:18] Priya Nair: hi i'm priya head of ml at delta labs, we own the assistant product and inference. tom here handles platform networking, anika is our security lead and luca is site reliability.
[00:35] Jose Ramirez: great, thanks. quick framing: we're focused on dedicated capacity for you given the isolation ask but we want to validate burst needs and SLAs. i'll ask a few infra questions then we'll talk sizing.
[00:50] Tom Barrett: sounds good. to be clear we are evaluating three modes: hosted for quick dev, dedicated for predictable capacity/isolation, and private for air-gapped customers. right now leaning dedicated.
[01:10] Maya Chen: yep exactly, and we often recommend dedicated for teams that need per-tenant isolation and consistent tail latencies. can you walk through your traffic profile?
[01:28] Priya Nair: baseline 300 rps across our assistant endpoints during work hours, but for product launches / marketing pushes we see spikes to 3k–4.5k rps for short windows — like 1–3 hours. that's usually the big ask: burst 10–15x.
[01:45] Jose Ramirez: okay that's helpful. and 95/99 latency SLOs?
[01:52] Priya Nair: 95th under 250ms and 99th under 600ms for text-only flows. multimodal flows longer, we accept 1.2s at 99p today.
[02:10] Luca Marino: also want predictable CPU/GPU tenancy — no noisy neighbor, so dedicated GPUs or single-tenant nodes are required for some customers.
[02:25] Anika Sood: on security we need SOC 2 Type II, SSO (SAML), KMS with BYOK, audit logs, and ability to hold logs for 1 year. can you confirm those are available on dedicated?
[02:40] Maya Chen: yes — Dedicated supports SAML, KMS integrations (BYOK/HSM), per-tenant audit logs and extended retention as an add-on. we can share the compliance pack after the call.
[02:52] Tom Barrett: how is isolation enforced? i.e., do we get physically separate nodes, gpu isolation by pool, or just network segregation?
[03:05] Jose Ramirez: good question. dedicated has a couple of isolation models: reserved GPU pools that you own logically and optionally physically isolated racks for stricter needs. most customers pick reserved pools with tenant-level runtime isolation + VPC peering — that's what gives predictable tail behavior without the cost of full racks.
[03:30] Priya Nair: cost tradeoff is important. if we reserve say N GPUs for baseline and need burst to 10x, what's the recommended pattern?
[03:42] Jose Ramirez: typically we recommend a two-layer approach: 1) reserved baseline pool sized for your steady-state, 2) a burst pool that can be auto-enabled in policy — could be warm standby nodes or preemptible instances depending on tolerance. we can model cost vs latency: warm-burst nodes cost more but give near-instant capacity; preemptible-style burst is cheaper but can have cold starts.
[04:10] Maya Chen: and we support automatic fallback routing: when dedicated burst is exhausted, you can failover to a smaller quantized model or to hosted capacity with throttles, depending on policy. that preserves availability while degrading quality gracefully.
[04:28] Tom Barrett: how long are warm nodes 'warm'? like how much KV cache or attention cache do we lose when spinning up new nodes?
[04:39] Jose Ramirez: the runtime uses KV cache on GPU and we do prefix cache warmup. a node that's been idle for >30 mins will need a brief warmup; for LLMs that can add ~100–400ms per request on first few calls. we recommend keeping a small set of warm warmers during peak windows.
[05:00] Priya Nair: hmm that 100–400ms could hurt our 95p target. can we keep a minimum of say 5 warm nodes during campaigns?
[05:12] Jose Ramirez: yes you can set min warmers and autoscale cooldown windows. the platform also supports pre-baking model snapshots so cold starts are faster.
[05:26] Anika Sood: on compliance, who has access to keys if we bring our own KMS? we need to ensure Redwood operators can't fetch plaintext.
[05:35] Maya Chen: with BYOK and customer-managed KMS, keys are in your control; Redwood obtains short-term access tokens for key usage only per-request, and we can provide audit records. we'll share the detailed KMS flow in the security pack.
[05:50] Luca Marino: what about network egress and peering? we need VPC peering and private endpoints.
[05:58] Jose Ramirez: dedicated supports VPC peering, private endpoints and egress control lists. for private deployments we also support on-prem bundles, but that moves control fully to you.
[06:15] Priya Nair: okay, let's talk numbers — assuming our baseline of 300 rps, multimodal mix 20% images, average token length 60, how many A100-equivalent GPUs would you recommend for reserved baseline?
[06:32] Jose Ramirez: rough rule of thumb depends on model. if you're running a 70B model on FP16, you'll get ~X tokens/sec per GPU. for token numbers you gave, we'd normally prototype. ballpark, for 300 rps text-only you might need ~6 A100-equivalents for steady state; with image-heavy multimodal that could go to 8–10. for peaks to 3k rps you'd want burst capacity in tens.
[07:00] Priya Nair: that's a big delta. how do customers usually handle burst—do they overcommit baseline or rely on burst pools?
[07:08] Maya Chen: many customers size baseline for normal operating hours and rely on burst pools that can be scheduled ahead for expected launches. if you have predictable marketing windows we can reserve burst capacity for those dates and charge lower than on-demand.
[07:24] Tom Barrett: what does the provisioning time look like for scheduled burst?
[07:30] Jose Ramirez: scheduled reserved burst is provisioned ahead of the date — think 24–72 hours depending on total capacity needed and regional availability. auto-scaling unplanned bursts can add capacity in minutes, but warm-up is the limiting factor.
[07:45] Priya Nair: for monthly launches we can reserve in advance. for unexpected virality we need fast failover to a hosted fallback. you said hosted fallback can be used — what are the quality tradeoffs?
[07:59] Maya Chen: hosted fallback gives access to compatible model variants in the Redwood catalog. we may route to a smaller quantized model, which reduces latency and cost but may change output style slightly. we also support function call routing and can tag invocations so you can run quality checks.
[08:20] Anika Sood: for the audit trail, do you emit request-level logs with user identifiers masked? we need PII controls.
[08:28] Jose Ramirez: yes, we have configurable PII redaction and you can opt to store only aggregated telemetry. request-level logs are optional and stored encrypted; redaction rules can be customer-defined.
[08:40] Priya Nair: what about autoscale policies — can we scale by QPS and by GPU utilization?
[08:48] Jose Ramirez: both. you can set scaling rules based on observed QPS, token throughput, GPU utilization, or a composite. cooldown windows and target utilization thresholds are adjustable.
[09:00] Luca Marino: how do you handle model rollouts? we need canary deploys and the ability to rollback instantly if quality regresses.
[09:09] Maya Chen: our rollout tooling supports canaries, percentage routing, A/B routing, and automatic rollback if quality or error rate thresholds are crossed. we integrate with your CI/CD and can store model versions and artifacts.
[09:25] Priya Nair: let's discuss instrumentation for the benchmark. what logs/metrics do you need from us?
[09:33] Jose Ramirez: for an apples-to-apples: request traces with token counts, sequence length distribution, QPS by route, 50/90/95/99 latencies, error rates, and a small labeled eval set for output quality checks. also network egress patterns for VPC sizing.
[09:50] Tom Barrett: any recommended synthetic traffic shape for simulating marketing bursts?
[09:55] Jose Ramirez: a mixed Poisson workload with a 10–15x short-tailed peak for 1–3 hours and gamma-distributed inter-arrival times for burstiness works well. we'll provide a script.
[10:12] Priya Nair: ok thanks. curious about cost-optimization — quantization vs batching vs caching — how do you recommend combining them?
[10:22] Jose Ramirez: tradeoffs: quantization reduces memory and often halves cost but may affect quality; batching improves throughput but increases tail latency for single requests; KV/prefix caching reduces per-token compute for repeated prompts. usually we suggest a mixed strategy: baseline using 8-bit quantized model with smart caching and aggressive batching for internal bulk workloads, and use higher-fidelity float models for high-SLA customer-facing flows.
[10:48] Anika Sood: is quantization compatible with your fallback models and hosted catalog?
[10:53] Jose Ramirez: yes, we maintain multiple model variants and will auto-select compatible fallbacks. we also test parity for key prompts during bench runs.
[11:05] Maya Chen: i'm going to flag two common patterns: 1) keep a minimal warm pool sized to maintain 95/99 targets; 2) schedule reserved burst for planned events. that combination usually hits both cost and latency targets.
[11:20] Priya Nair: okay good to know. now on pricing — i'm guessing reserved GPUs are a monthly commit and burst is hourly or event-based?
[11:30] Maya Chen: yes reserved is monthly/annual commit. burst can be scheduled as reserved short-term (for a discount) or on a consumption basis. we'll include concrete numbers in the playbook.
[11:42] Tom Barrett: for the benchmark, can we run it in our VPC or do we need a test project in Redwood?
[11:49] Jose Ramirez: we can do both. recommended: run initial benchmark in Redwood's dedicated staging with VPC peering so we can control telemetry and then validate in your VPC for networking/firewall constraints.
[12:02] Priya Nair: how do you instrument model quality during the bench? do you collect semantic similarity or human eval lines?
[12:10] Jose Ramirez: we'll run a labeled eval set and compute automated metrics (BLEU/ROUGE for structured, embedding-similarity for freeform) plus spot human review for 1–2k samples. quality thresholds you define will be monitored during run.
[12:28] Anika Sood: patching and maintenance — who handles kernel updates or patched libs on dedicated nodes?
[12:36] Maya Chen: Redwood manages OS and runtime patches for hosted and dedicated; for physically isolated racks we can coordinate maintenance windows. for private/on-prem, you manage updates unless you include the managed service add-on.
[12:51] Luca Marino: what's the SLA for Dedicated?
[12:55] Maya Chen: typical SLA is 99.9% for Reserved Dedicated with credits and 99.95% available for enterprise tiers. exact SLA will be in the contract.
[13:06] Priya Nair: okay let's talk about a concrete pilot: what would you recommend for a 2-week pilot to validate cost and tail latency?
[13:16] Jose Ramirez: pilot plan: provision a small dedicated pool sized for 30–40% of baseline (to save cost), configure warmers, run a 48-hour steady-state test, then replay a 3-hour synthetic peak at 10x while collecting 50/90/95/99 latency and quality metrics. include canary rollback tests and fallback routing to hosted.
[13:38] Maya Chen: duration 2 weeks gives us time to iterate on warmers and quantization choices. we'll supply the runbook and stage keys.
[13:48] Tom Barrett: will the pilot require changes to our code path? we prefer minimal integration work.
[13:55] Jose Ramirez: no heavy change. we expose the same REST/SDK endpoints; you can change routing and models via config. the only extra is agent for generating telemetry and VPC peering setup.
[14:09] Priya Nair: can Redwood sign an NDA and share more detailed architecture diagrams and cost model?
[14:15] Maya Chen: yes we'll sign the NDA. i'll attach the contract and security pack in follow-up email.
[14:23] Anika Sood: one more: for data residency — we need logs kept in EU for EU customers. can dedicated region pinning be done?
[14:33] Jose Ramirez: region pinning is supported; you can pin workloads to region and control where logs are stored.
[14:42] Priya Nair: ok great. any outstanding risks you see from your side?
[14:48] Jose Ramirez: biggest risk is under-sizing warmers causing tail spikes during burst. second is network egress bumps for multimodal data — both manageable with the pilot.
[15:00] Luca Marino: people ask about preemption — if we use cheaper preemptible burst nodes how often do they get reclaimed and what's the expected impact?
[15:09] Jose Ramirez: preemptible nodes are reclaimed on a best-effort basis; they work for asynchronous batch jobs more than low-latency inference. for real-time you want warm or scheduled reserved burst.
[15:20] Priya Nair: for vendor comparisons — we also looked at Anthropic and a self-hosted Triton stack. what are Redwood's strengths vs those?
[15:30] Maya Chen: compared to Anthropic (hosted-centric), we offer unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private and deeper orchestration for reserved bursts. vs Triton self-host, we provide the orchestration, autoscale, and observability — so you don't build the ops layer.
[15:46] Priya Nair: ok, makes sense.
[15:50] Maya Chen: quick recap and proposed timeline: we run a 2-week pilot starting next week, benchmarking limited steady state + one scheduled 3-hour peak. post-pilot we size a production reserved baseline, and define reserved burst dates for the next 3 months.
[16:05] Priya Nair: sounds good — we'll confirm dates and send traffic profiles.
[16:12] Tom Barrett: and please include the network checklist for VPC peering.
[16:16] Maya Chen: will do. any final questions?
[16:20] Anika Sood: please include a redaction policy example in the security pack.
[16:24] Maya Chen: yep adding that to the pack.
[16:28] Priya Nair: thanks everyone.
[16:30] Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up with materials and schedule the infra deep-dive.

Recap (spoken at end):
- Pilot: 2 weeks, small dedicated pool + scheduled 3-hour 10x replay; collect 50/90/95/99 latencies and quality metrics.
- Deliverables: pricing + isolation whitepaper (Maya), benchmark runbook (Jose), Delta Labs traffic profile (Priya).
- Tentative dates: tech deep-dive week of 2026-05-11, pilot start week of 2026-05-18 (to be confirmed).

Links mentioned: Redwood Dedicated whitepaper (link sent post-call), benchmark script (will be shared), security pack (NDA required).
